## Introduction

### N170 Component Characteristics
The polarity of the N170 ERP is negative, displaying a voltage peak at a latency of approximately 170ms post-stimulus onset (Gao et al., 2019). The most topographically active areas when the N170 is elicited are the bilateral occipito-temporal areas, specifically, electrodes P7, P8, PO7 and PO8 with a standard 10-20 system (Johnston et al., 2015; Navajas et al., 2013). 

### Background Research on the N170 Component
#### Initial Observations of the N170
The N170 was first officially observed by Bentin et al. (1996), utilising electrodes to study facial perception. Bentin et al. (1996) found that pictures of a human face elicited an N170 at approximately 172ms, located most prominently over the posterior temporal scalp and displayed greater prominence over the right hemisphere. Bentin et al. (1996) found that distorted faces displayed the same N170 amplitude and latency as normal faces, while inverted faces produced the same amplitude for the N170 as upright faces, despite a slight time delay. Interestingly, Bentin et al. (1996) found that sole depiction of human eyes elicited an N170 of greater amplitude compared to display of the whole face, while depiction of the nose and lips displayed a 50ms delay of the N170, alongside a decreased amplitude than that of the whole face. A distinct difference is that the N170 was not elicited by animal’s faces, human hands or inanimate objects, positing that the N170 may reflect the brain’s recognition of human faces, and specifically, eye recognition (Bentin et al., 1996).

Despite the first formal publication of the N170 from Bentin et al. (1996), Bötzel & Grüsser (1989) observed the first findings related to facial perceptions through a component now known as the Vertex Positive Potential (VPP). Bötzel & Grüsser (1989) observed the VPP after displaying human faces amongst control objects such as chairs and trees. The VPP occurred at electrode Cz between 150ms to 200ms post-stimulus onset of the visual display of human faces. Through use of a larger number of electrodes, Bötzel et al. (1995) found that the VPP was a direct three-dimensional correspondent to the N170 found at the occipito-temporal sites. Finally, Bötzel et al. (1995) undertook advanced computer analysis of dipoles, finding that the electrical signals originated deep in the temporal cortex, crossing the visual cortex and centre of the scalp. Prior to Bötzel & Grüsser’s (1989) use of electroencephalography (EEG) to understand human facial processing, researchers largely relied on animal studies and research with prosopagnosia patients. Thus, the works of Bötzel & Grüsser (1989) mark important methodological advances in understanding the processes behind human facial processing.

#### Conditions where the N170 Component is elicited
The classic visual stimuli utilised to elicit the N170 ERP component is human facial stimuli (Eimer, 2011). Inverted human faces have also elicited the N170 component, however, with an increased amplitude and delayed deflection compared to visual display of an upright human face (Civile et al., 2018). Different human facial expressions, such as fear, have also been seen to inflate the negative amplitude of the N170 response (Blau et al., 2007). While human facial features elicit the N170, the eyes elicit a larger amplitude of the N170 compared to a whole upright human face, alongside delayed latency than that of features such as the nose and mouth. 

The N170 ERP component is particularly sensitive to facial visual stimuli but can also be elicited by written words (Eimer, 2011; Maurer et al., 2005). 

#### Functional Significance of the N170 Component
The Face Perception Paradigm is an electroencephalographic experiment utilised to evoke an N170 ERP component (Yildirim-Keles et al., 2025). The N170 is a functionally significant ERP component that is thought to represent visual facial detection and encoding in a gestalt manner (Olivares et al., 2015). The N170 ERP is generally evoked by presenting participants with visual stimuli of faces amongst visual stimuli of objects, providing a relative ‘baseline’ between facial and non-facial visual stimuli (Rossion, 2014).

#### Epoching parameters

```{python}
TMIN = -0.2 # epoch start relative to critical event
TMAX = 0.8  # epoch end relative to critical event

BASELINE = (-0.2,0) # baseline interval

# critical conditions for averaging and epoching
CONDITIONS = ["stimulus/face", "stimulus/car", "stimulus/scrambled_face", "stimulus/scrambled_car"]

REJECT = {
    "eeg": 150e-6,
    "eog": 250e-6
}

```

## Data analysis

### Preprocessing

```{python}
#| eval: true # set this to false if you don't want preprocessing to recompute
#| output: false # this suppresses any output

for raw_file in RAW_PATH.glob("*_raw.fif.gz"):

    # extract subject number
    subj_ID = raw_file.stem.split("_")[0]

    # read in raw file 
    raw = SimpleRaw(raw_file)

    # preprocess raw file
    # note how we draw on a custom preprocessing function here
    processed = preprocess(raw, 
                            reref_params = REFERENCE, 
                            filter_low_cutoff = FILTER_SETTINGS["low_cutoff"], 
                            filter_high_cutoff = FILTER_SETTINGS["high_cutoff"])
    
    processed.save(PROCESSED_PATH / f"{subj_ID}_raw.fif.gz", overwrite = True)


```

### Epoching and averaging

```{python}
#| output: false

# initialise empty dictionary to hold single-subject averages
ss_avs = {}

for cond in CONDITIONS:
    ss_avs[cond] = []

for processed_file in PROCESSED_PATH.glob("*_raw.fif.gz"):

    subj_ID = processed_file.stem.split("_")[0]
    print(f"processing participant {subj_ID}")

    if subj_ID in EXCLUDE:
        continue
    
    # read in preprocessed file
    processed = SimpleRaw(processed_file)

    # extract events
    events, event_id = processed.get_events()

    # epoch data
    epochs = SimpleEpoch(processed, events, event_id, tmin = TMIN, tmax = TMAX, baseline = BASELINE, reject = REJECT)

    # subset epochs and average by condition 
    for cond in CONDITIONS:
        av = epochs[cond].average()
        ss_avs[cond].append(av)

```

### Grand average

```{python}
#| output: false

# create an empty dict to hold our grand averages
grand_avs = {}

for cond in CONDITIONS:
    grand = grand_average(ss_avs[cond])
    grand_avs[cond] = grand
```
